latin.335: Adstringitur vis consequentiae si haec instantia ad Propositionem S. Coenae: Hoc est Corpus meum, applicetur, per id scil., quòd Christus S. Coenam immediàte post Pascha celebratum instituturus & commendaturus discipulis mysteriorum divinorum perquam ignaris, non potuit voluisse verba sua: Hoc, i. e. hic panis est corpus meum, aliter ab iis intelligi, quàm verba vixdum celebrati paschalis, Hoc, i. e. hic agnus est pascha seu transitus, ab iisdem intellecta hactenus erant, praesertim, cùm adderet Christus, quod pro vobis vel fractum est, vel frangitur, quôve sensu accipi debebat posterior propositio Christi Eucharistica: Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo qui pro vobis effunditur; Secus, & quodsi vel aliter intelligi verba sua à discipulis voluisse Christus, vel discipuli eadem aliter intellexissent, tam Christus iis admodum obscurè locutus fuisset, quam ipsis ansa suppeditata, ad miras quaestiones dilabendi, similes iis, quae leguntur Joh. cap. 14.
latin.336: Quando (y) in definitivis Baptismatis nonnullis: Baptisma est indutio Christi Gal. 3. 27. item, est ἐπερώτημα συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς εἰς Θεόν 1. Petr. 3. Spiritus S. sola Baptismatis Signata, de Signo, sive nudo, i. e. baptismate externo, sive exhibitivo, i. e. de integro baptismo, ex interna & externa parte constante, praedicat, negari nequit, vel Metonymicam vel Synechdochicam praedicationem fieri.
latin.337: Denique (d) Cùm in Institutionis S. Coenae parte altera propositio, tùm à Christo primum enunciata, apud Lucam cap. 22. vers. 20. tùm ab Apostolo 1. Cor. 11. vers. 25. repetita, occurrit: Poculum est N. T. in sanguine Christi, unô eam plures tropos spirare nemo facilè inficias ibit, ne quidem Pontificius Cajetanus in Luc. 22. ex Thoma de Aquino 1. Cor. 10.; quin potius Gregorius de Valencia etiam necessitatem tropi agnoscet de Eucharistia Libro I. cap. 9. th. 42. ita scribens: In propositione, Hic calix est N. T. in sanguine meo, oportere prorsus calicem accipi pro re contenta, quae est Christi Sanguis; & consequenter, de hoc sanguine testamentum, seu promissionem, non nisi figurate praedicari, quatenus promissionem videl. & Testamentum confirmat, ut explicat ille dicendi modus Matthaei & Marci in casu nominis obliquo, sanguis Novi Testamenti.
latin.338: Nec abnuet Lutheranus quivis, certè non Dominus Daniel Severinus Scultetus in Discussione Universalismi Reformati adhuc recenti, consequentiam interim abnuens: Ponam inquit, in his verbis (partis scil. Institutionis sacrae Coenae, secundae, seu posterioris) esse tropum, non sunt eam ob causam reliqua ad Sacrae Eucharistiae institutionem pertinentia tropicè accipienda. Proprius enim verborum sensus ubivis est retinendus, ni gravis obstet causa, quae hic, scilicet in propositione prioris Partis: Hoc est corpus meum, nulla est. Quibus verbis, uti mihi consenserit Clariss. vir, propositionem Eucharisticam: Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo, tropô non uno constare, tantôque magis consenserit, non nude posuerit, quantô ex Hebr. cap. 9. vers. 17. & 20. magis annotaverit, modum hunc loquendi aemulari formulam dicendi Mosis, cùm populum totum expiaret, & sanguine aspergeret, ita sonantem: Hic est sanguis N. T. à Deo injuncti;
latin.339: Ita vicissim me sibi duplici modo habuerit consentientem, tùm quod ex dictae propositionis (Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo) improprietate admissâ, non sequatur, omnia reliqua, ad S. Eucharistiae institutionem pertinentia verba, tropicè sumenda; tùm quòd proprius verborum sensus ubivis retinendus sit, nisi gravis obstet causa; dummodo praetereà observare haud gravetur Dominus Scultetus (1) me non ex propositione impropria hac: Hoc poculum est Novum Testamentum, inferre vel voluisse, vel etiamnum velle, omnia S. Coenae institutionis verba impropria esse, sed dicere duntaxat: Definitiva Sacramentalia adeo non abhorrere ab improprietate, ut ex omnium in universum (exceptis tantisper his solis; Hoc est corpus meum) improprietate, citra controversiam admittenda, probabilissimè saltem, & horum inferri queat improprietas. (2) Dictam modò improprietatem, postremis hisce necessariò transcribendam esse, quòd gravissima proprietati eorum causa obstet, quâ gravior dari nequit, ea scil. qua alioquin futurum est, ut Disparatum de Disparato, contra omnem hujus naturam sanamque hominum rationem, propriè praedicari dicendum fuerit.
latin.340:
§. IV.
Argumenta, specificam propositionis, de qua adhuc disquiritur, naturam attingentia, istorum potissimum testimoniis conficiuntur, qui improprietatem ejus in specie, vel disertè atque explicitè, vel per interpretationes suas, sicque implicite, agnoscunt ac confitentur. EXPLICITE figuratam statuunt (1) PATRES ECCLESIAE ANTIQUIORES, quorum testimonia summâ industriâ collegit ex primis Reformatoribus Oecolampadius, in Dialogo, Melanchton, in consilio Epistolico, ad Fridericum Palatinum misso; Ex recentioribus Johannes Jonstonus Reformatus Syntag. de Commun. veteris Ecclesiae cap. 3. art. 3. §. 3. à pag. mihi 86. ad pag. 100. Et Petrus Picherellus Pontificius Opuscul. Theol. p. 28.

pass_a.335: The force of the consequence is tightened if this instance is applied to the Proposition of the Sacred Supper This is my Body — namely because Christ, about to institute and commend the Sacred Supper immediately after the Passover had been celebrated to disciples quite ignorant of the divine mysteries, could not have willed His words This, i.e. this bread is my body, to be understood by them otherwise than the words of the Passover just celebrated, This, i.e. this lamb is the passover or passage, had hitherto been understood by the same — especially when Christ added what is broken or is being broken for you, and in which sense the posterior Eucharistic proposition of Christ was to be taken: This cup is the N.T. in my blood which is poured out for you; Otherwise, and if either Christ had willed His words to be understood otherwise by the disciples, or the disciples had understood the same otherwise, Christ would have spoken to them quite obscurely, and a handle would have been supplied them for sliding into wondrous questions like those read in John ch. 14.
pass_a.336: When (y) in some Baptismal definitives: Baptism is the putting on of Christ, Gal. 3:27; also, it is the appeal of a good conscience toward God, 1 Pet. 3 — the Holy Spirit predicates only the Signified things of Baptism of the Sign, whether bare, i.e. the external baptism, or exhibitive, i.e. of the whole baptism consisting of internal and external part — it cannot be denied that a Metonymic or Synechdochic predication is made.
pass_a.337: Finally (d) When in the other part of the Institution of the Sacred Supper the proposition occurs, both first uttered by Christ in Luke 22:20 and repeated by the Apostle in 1 Cor. 11:25: The Cup is the N.T. in the blood of Christ — no one will easily deny that it breathes several tropes in one, not even the Pontifician Cajetan on Luke 22 from Thomas Aquinas on 1 Cor. 10; nay rather Gregory of Valencia will also acknowledge the necessity of a trope concerning the Eucharist, Book I ch. 9 th. 42, writing thus: In the proposition This cup is the N.T. in my blood, the cup must altogether be taken for the contained thing, which is Christ’s Blood; and consequently testament or promise is predicated of this blood only figuratively, inasmuch as it confirms the promise and Testament — as that mode of speaking of Matthew and Mark explains in the oblique case, blood of the New Testament.
pass_a.338: Nor will any Lutheran deny it — certainly not Dom. Daniel Severinus Scultetus in the still recent Discussion of Reformed Universalism, meanwhile denying the consequence: I will grant, he says, that in these words (namely of the second or posterior part of the Institution of the Sacred Supper) there is a trope; the remaining things pertaining to the Institution of the Sacred Eucharist are not for that reason to be taken tropically. For the proper sense of words is everywhere to be retained unless a grave cause obstructs, which here — namely in the proposition of the prior Part This is my body — there is none. With which words, as the most distinguished man will have agreed with me that the Eucharistic proposition This cup is the N.T. in my blood consists of not one trope, so much the more will he have agreed, not having merely posited it, the more he will have annotated from Heb. 9:17 & 20 that this mode of speaking emulates Moses’ formula when he purified the whole people and sprinkled them with blood, sounding thus: This is the blood of the N.T. enjoined by God;
pass_a.339: So in turn he will have me consenting to him in a double way — both that from the admitted impropriety of the said proposition (This cup is the N.T. in my blood) it does not follow that all the remaining words pertaining to the Institution of the Sacred Eucharist are to be taken tropically; and that the proper sense of words is everywhere to be retained unless a grave cause obstructs — provided Dom. Scultetus will not be unwilling further to observe (1) that I have not wished, nor do I still wish, to infer from this improper proposition This cup is the New Testament that all the words of the Institution of the Sacred Supper are improper, but only to say: Definitive Sacramentals so little abhor impropriety that from the impropriety of all of them in general (excepting for a while only these: This is my body), to be admitted without controversy, the impropriety of these too can at least most probably be inferred. (2) That the impropriety just named must necessarily be transcribed to these last, because a most grave cause obstructs their propriety — than which none graver can be given — namely that otherwise it will come about that a Disparate must be said to be predicated properly of a Disparate, against all the nature of this and sound human reason.
pass_a.340: §. IV. The arguments touching the specific nature of the proposition still under inquiry are chiefly made up from the testimonies of those who acknowledge and confess its impropriety in species, either expressly and explicitly, or through their interpretations and so implicitly. EXPLICITLY they establish it as figurative (1) the MORE ANCIENT FATHERS OF THE CHURCH, whose testimonies with greatest industry Oecolampadius among the first Reformers collected in a Dialogue, Melanchthon in an Epistolary counsel sent to Frederick the Palatine; Among more recent writers Johannes Jonstonus the Reformed, Syntagma on the Communion of the ancient Church ch. 3 art. 3 §. 3 from p. to me 86 to p. 100. And Petrus Picherellus the Pontifician, Theological Opuscula p. 28.

335: Tighten the consequence by applying that Passover instance to This is my Body.
Christ was instituting the Supper right after Passover for disciples still raw in the divine mysteries.

He cannot have meant This bread is my body to be heard differently from This lamb is the passover / passage — especially with broken for you and This cup is the N.T. in my blood poured out for you — or else He would have spoken obscurely and opened John-14-style puzzles.
336: (y) In some baptismal definitives — Baptism is putting on Christ (Gal. 3:27); it is the appeal of a good conscience toward God (1 Pet. 3) — the Spirit predicates only Baptism’s signified things of the sign.
Whether the sign is bare external baptism or the whole exhibitive rite, the predication is metonymic or synechdochic; that cannot be denied.
337: (d) In the other half of the Supper Institution — Luke 22:20 and 1 Cor. 11:25 — The Cup is the N.T. in Christ’s blood.
No one easily denies that one line breathes several tropes — not even Cajetan.

Gregory of Valencia grants the necessity: the cup must be taken for the contained blood, and testament/promise is predicated of that blood only figuratively (as Matthew and Mark’s blood of the New Testament shows).
338: Scultetus, in his recent Discussion of Reformed Universalism, grants a trope in those second-part Institution words, yet denies the consequence for the rest of the Eucharist Institution.
Proper sense, he says, is kept everywhere unless a grave cause blocks it — and in This is my body, he claims, there is none.
Strimesius notes he already agrees the Cup proposition is built of more than one trope, and all the more once Heb. 9:17, 20 shows it emulates Moses’ This is the blood of the N.T.
339: So Strimesius consents on two points: admitting Cup impropriety does not make every other Institution word tropical; and proper sense stays unless a grave cause blocks it.

(1) He does not infer from This cup is the New Testament that all Supper Institution words are improper — only that definitive sacramentals so little abhor impropriety that from all the rest (This is my body set aside for now) one may most probably infer these too are improper.

(2) That impropriety must be written onto This is my body as well, because the gravest cause blocks propriety: otherwise a Disparate would have to be predicated properly of a Disparate against nature and sound reason.
340: §. IV. Arguments for the specific nature of the proposition under debate are drawn chiefly from those who acknowledge its impropriety in species — expressly, or implicitly by their interpretations.
EXPLICITLY figurative: the more ancient Church Fathers (collected by Oecolampadius and Melanchthon), the Reformed Jonstonus, and the Pontifician Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 28).
